assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed the foundations of trade theory. It moved the field from representative-firm models to productivity-sorted exporters, and it reshaped both empirical work and trade policy analysis. The theory is closely tied to firm-level data, which is the type of work I value.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central model. Helpman supplied the monopolistic-competition foundations and the later firm-level extensions. Redding is a major later contributor, but his work is more recent and more quantitative. Credit also overlaps with the empirical firm-exporter literature, which is not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation. The framework is standard in graduate teaching and in quantitative trade policy evaluation. The work is mature.
uncertainties: Helpman has other claims (B049), and the committee may prefer a different grouping.
Prior empirical work on exporter premia that is not among the credited names could complicate attribution.
Trade already has several recent laureates, which may affect the field balance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed how economists and policymakers think about labour demand, automation, trade adjustment and wage inequality. The topic is important and the empirical work is credible.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Hanson are central to the local labour-market effects of trade. Katz is central to the long-run work on skill demand and supply. Dorn is a key co-author of the China shock papers, but the three-name limit forces a choice. The task-based theory has other originators, including Acemoglu, who has already been recognised.
assessment.maturity: The work spans about 25 years. The China shock literature is more recent but heavily replicated and debated, and its policy influence is substantial.
uncertainties: Katz also appears in B050 and has a different set of co-authors in the skill-premium work.
Some of the China shock identification and magnitude claims remain contested.
The 2024 prize for institutions and the 2021 prize for natural experiments may overlap in subject matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: These economists built the modern formal and empirical study of how political institutions shape economic policy and outcomes. Their work covers electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal outcomes. The program is coherent, and it combines theory with a large body of empirical testing.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core of the constitutional and electoral-rule work, and Besley is central to the state-capacity and accountability literature. The attribution is natural and fairly clean for these three names. Other contributors to the broader political-economy field, such as Acemoglu and Robinson, are already or partly recognised.
assessment.maturity: The work spans three decades, with a mature literature and wide use in policy analysis.
uncertainties: Persson's Stockholm affiliation and long overlap with committee members is a conflict that should be disclosed. I do not adjudicate it here.
The 2024 prize may reduce appetite for another institutions-related award.
Empirical identification in the cross-country constitutional work is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference have become part of applied economics. The key tools include double/debiased ML, causal forests and heterogeneous treatment effect estimation. These methods are widely used in economics, in policy evaluation and in technology firms.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov's double ML and Athey's work on causal forests and policy learning are both strongly credited. Wager is a key co-author of the causal forest work, but he is junior to the others. Related contributions from Imbens, Belloni, Hansen and others complicate the credit.
assessment.maturity: The work is roughly 8 to 12 years old. Adoption is rapid, but the long-run test of the methods has not yet been completed.
uncertainties: The methods are young relative to typical Nobel timing.
Imbens and Angrist have already been recognised for related work, so the committee may think the area is covered.
The credit is spread across many authors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of demand with differentiated products, together with dynamic models of industries, changed empirical IO, antitrust and merger analysis. The methods are used extensively in competition policy, and the contribution is both methodological and practical.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is clearly identified with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes is also central to dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) and productivity estimation. Bresnahan and Reiss made important earlier contributions, which complicates the three-name limit.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates to 1995. It has three decades of use in both academic work and policy, so the confirmation is strong.
uncertainties: Bresnahan and Reiss could reasonably argue for inclusion, so attribution is uncertain.
The committee has recognised IO and market design before and may weigh field balance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data changed how economists measure mobility, neighbourhood effects and the effects of policy. The research is empirically influential and has shaped policy debate. It also created a large new data-driven research program.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leader and common thread across the work, with Hendren, Friedman and Katz as principal co-authors on different strands. A single-laureate selection is the cleanest option, but it leaves out co-authors on the key mobility papers.
assessment.maturity: The main work is about 10 to 15 years old. Some findings have been replicated, but long-run validation and the debates about causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects are still developing.
uncertainties: The work is relatively young for a Nobel.
Some identification and measurement choices in the mobility estimates are contested.
Credit is heavily shared across a large team.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law and finance program showed that legal origins and investor protection are linked to financial development and ownership structure. This agenda changed corporate finance, comparative law and development debates. It is influential in both academic and policy settings, including the corporate governance reforms I know from my own field.
assessment.attribution: The core work is La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny (LLSV). A three-name limit excludes Vishny, who is a co-author of the foundational papers, which is a real attribution difficulty. Shleifer has other prize-relevant contributions, including behavioural finance.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly 30 years old. Later critiques have revised the legal origins interpretation, but the core empirical regularities remain central.
uncertainties: Subsequent research has challenged the identification and the legal-origin interpretation.
The credit split among the four authors is uncomfortable.
Shleifer's non-research controversies may matter to the committee, though they are not part of my assessment of merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework and the Taylor rule became the working basis for modern monetary policy analysis and central bank practice. The work has major practical and theoretical impact across the field.
assessment.attribution: Credit is highly diffuse. Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts), Woodford (the integrated framework), Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, and Smets (estimated DSGE models) all made central contributions. A three-name limit cannot capture the full distribution, so the choice here is only a plausible subset.
assessment.maturity: The work is 25 to 40 years old and thoroughly tested. The 2008 and 2020s inflation episodes have prompted useful re-examination and refinement.
uncertainties: The attribution is the main weakness, as the credit could easily be split in other ways.
Previous recognition of related macroeconomics (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims, Bernanke et al.) could reduce the appeal.
Questions about the framework's performance in recent inflation episodes remain.
